opus-5.5.text:
I think it would change biology at a pretty fundamental level, because right now so much of the field is descriptive. We're incredibly good at cataloguing things: we sequence genomes, we profile cells, we image tissues, we build atlases. But if you ask a biologist to predict what happens when you perturb a system, say knock out a gene or add a drug or combine three mutations, most of the time the honest answer is "we have to run the experiment and see."

Compare that to physics or chemistry, where you can often reason forward from first principles and get a pretty good answer before you ever touch a pipette. Biology has never really had that. It's been an empirical, trial-and-error science, partly because the systems are so complex and so context-dependent that no human can hold all the variables in their head.

So if we get models that can actually predict, with real accuracy, how a cell responds to a perturbation, or how a protein sequence maps to function, or how a regulatory change propagates through a network, then biology starts to look more like an engineering discipline. You'd move from "let's screen ten thousand things and hope something works" to "let's design the thing we want, simulate it, and test the handful of candidates most likely to succeed." The wet lab doesn't go away. It becomes the place where you validate and generate the data that makes the models better, a tight loop between computation and experiment.

I think it also changes what counts as understanding. Historically, understanding in biology meant you could tell a mechanistic story: this protein binds that one, which activates this pathway. Predictive models might work even when we can't fully articulate the mechanism. That's a bit uncomfortable for a field built on narrative explanations, but I think it's ultimately freeing. You can then use the model as an instrument to probe *why* it makes the predictions it does, and that becomes a new way of generating hypotheses.

And practically, the payoff is enormous. Drug discovery, where most candidates fail in the clinic, is fundamentally a prediction problem. Cell engineering, gene therapy, figuring out which variants in your genome actually matter: all of these get transformed if we can simulate biology instead of just observing it. That's really the big shift: from biology as a science of observation to biology as a science of design.

r001.rationale: The response describes biology as empirical and trial-and-error, saying researchers often have to run experiments to see what happens after a perturbation.

r002.rationale: It discusses experimental validation and biology’s empirical nature, but does not identify a requirement for demonstrated evidence as a constraint on speculation in scientific papers.

r003.rationale: It predicts a fundamental shift from observation and trial-and-error toward design, and says predictive models could change what counts as understanding in biology.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it would change biology from a discipline that's fundamentally descriptive into one that's actually predictive and engineerable, and that's a really profound shift.

If you think about how biology has worked for most of its history, it's been about observation. You look through a microscope, you sequence a genome, you run a screen, and you catalog what you see. We've gotten incredibly good at measuring things. But the gap has always been that you can't really reason forward from first principles the way a physicist or an engineer can. You can't sit down and say, if I make this edit to this gene in this cell type, here is exactly what will happen to the phenotype. You have to go do the experiment. And experiments are slow, they're expensive, and they fail most of the time.

So the core limitation is that biology has never really had a theory in the sense that physics has one. We have the central dogma, we have evolution, and those are organizing frameworks, but they don't let you compute an answer. What's exciting about these models is that they could become something like that missing theory, except it's learned from data rather than written down as equations. A model that has seen millions of genomes and billions of sequences has implicitly absorbed the rules that evolution has been running experiments against for billions of years.

Once you have that, a few things happen. First, the loop between hypothesis and experiment gets dramatically tighter, because you run thousands of experiments in silico and only take the most promising ones to the bench. The wet lab becomes a validation step rather than a search step. Second, it changes who gets to do biology. Right now, a lot of what makes a great biologist is accumulated intuition that takes a decade to develop. If some of that intuition lives in a model, you can lower the barrier for people coming from engineering or computer science to contribute meaningfully. And third, I think it changes the questions we ask. When you can design rather than just discover, you start asking what should exist rather than only what does exist. You can design a protein or a genetic circuit or a therapy that nature never produced.

I'd also say it changes the sociology of the field. Biology today is organized around model systems and individual labs with deep expertise in one organism or one pathway. A predictive model doesn't care about those boundaries. It can transfer what it learned from bacteria to what it needs to know about human cells. So I think we'll see biology become more like a platform science, where there's shared infrastructure, foundation models, large datasets generated specifically to train them, and then a lot of people building on top of that.

The caveat is that the models are only as good as the data, and biological data has historically been collected to answer narrow questions, not to train general models. So part of the work ahead is rethinking how we generate data at scale, with the model in mind from the start. But if we get that right, I genuinely think biology in twenty years looks less like natural history and more like engineering.

r001.rationale: The response describes biology as requiring experiments to find out what an intervention does, with experiments slow, expensive, and often unsuccessful—characterizing research as a trial-and-error process.

r002.rationale: It discusses biology’s reliance on experiments, but does not say that demands for empirical evidence constrain speculation in scientific papers.

r003.rationale: It predicts a change in the field’s sociology and organization, including a shift toward shared infrastructure and platform science.

astra-6.text:
I think they would change the relationship between experimentation and understanding. In biology, we spend an enormous amount of effort measuring things, finding correlations, and then doing experiments to figure out which relationships are causal. A model that could reliably predict what happens when you perturb a gene or change a cell’s environment would let you explore many more possibilities before you ever walk into the lab.

That could move biology toward being a more predictive engineering discipline. You could start with a desired outcome—say, a cell that performs a particular therapeutic function—and work backward to the changes you need to make, rather than screening huge numbers of possibilities and hoping you find something useful.

But the key question is what those predictions generalize to. Predicting another example that looks like your training data is very different from predicting an intervention in a biological context you’ve never seen. Experiments would still be essential, both to test those predictions and to discover where the model breaks down. Ideally, you get a much faster cycle: models help you choose the most informative experiments, and those experiments make the models better.

r001.rationale: The response describes researchers screening many possibilities and hoping to find something useful, while using experiments to work out causal relationships—an account of trial and error.

r002.rationale: It says experiments remain essential for testing predictions, but does not discuss scientific papers or empirical evidence limiting speculation in them.

r003.rationale: It predicts a shift toward predictive engineering, with models guiding experiments and experiments improving models, describing a change in biology’s research culture.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they could shift biology from a primarily descriptive science toward a much more predictive and engineering-oriented discipline. We’re very good at measuring biological systems and cataloging their parts, but it’s still difficult to predict what happens when you change something. If I perturb this gene, what happens to the cell? If I change this sequence, what happens to the protein? And does that prediction hold in a different context?

If we could answer those questions reliably, we could start designing experiments around the outcomes we want, rather than screening enormous numbers of possibilities. That would change how we discover drugs, engineer cells, and understand disease.

But prediction wouldn’t eliminate experiments. It would make them more valuable. You’d want to do the experiments that distinguish between competing explanations, or reveal where the model breaks. Ideally, you get this feedback loop where models guide experiments, experiments improve models, and our ability to understand and engineer biology gets progressively better.

r001.rationale: The response describes biology as difficult to predict and says researchers often screen enormous numbers of possibilities, conveying a largely trial-and-error approach.

r002.rationale: It says experiments remain important, but does not discuss empirical evidence constraining speculation in scientific papers.

r003.rationale: It predicts a shift toward predictive, engineering-oriented biology, with models guiding experiments and changing how discoveries are made.
